planting.note: Seed benefits from a moist cold stratification of 60-90 days, so fall sowing outdoors or a refrigerated stratification before spring sowing gives the most reliable germination.

directions: Grow in gritty, fast-draining, lean soil in full sun to very light afternoon shade at elevation, mimicking the subalpine meadows and rocky slopes of the central and southern Rockies where this species is native. Unlike most beardtongues, the tubular flowers open pale greenish-cream and age to smoky dusky purple or maroon, giving each raceme a distinctive two-toned look that draws bumblebees and other native pollinators. Plants resent summer humidity and heavy clay, so a rock garden or scree bed with excellent winter drainage suits it best. Avoid supplemental fertilizer, which produces lax, floppy growth in this naturally compact alpine species.

common_name: Gilia Beardtongue (Prairie Baby's Breath, Bush Penstemon)

planting.note: Direct sow after danger of hard frost into sandy, low-fertility soil; established plants are drought-tough but young seedlings need occasional water their first season.

directions: Plant in deep sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; this shrubby, much-branched beardtongue of the Chihuahuan Desert and southern High Plains forms a low mound studded with masses of small, net-veined white to pale pink flowers that give it a haze reminiscent of baby's breath from a distance. It tolerates true desert heat and alkaline soils that defeat most other Penstemon species, and needs no irrigation once roots are established. The airy mounding habit works well trailing over rock walls or softening the edge of a xeriscape bed, and the abundant small flowers attract native bees and occasional hummingbird visits through a long summer bloom season. Avoid rich garden soil and overhead watering, both of which shorten the plant's lifespan.
sources: Native Plant Society of New Mexico

planting.note: Fall sowing or fall transplanting is preferred in the low desert Southwest so roots establish through the mild winter ahead of the spring bloom flush.

directions: Grow in rocky or sandy, sharply draining alkaline soil in full sun, conditions typical of the Sonoran Desert foothills and washes this species calls home. Tall, slender wands of bright magenta-pink tubular flowers rise well above a basal rosette of blue-green leaves in a dramatic late-winter to spring bloom that is one of the earliest nectar sources for migrating hummingbirds in Arizona gardens. Plants are often short-lived perennials that reseed readily, so allowing some seed to drop keeps a planting going for years. Water sparingly through summer dormancy and avoid soil amendments or heavy mulch, which promote crown rot in the desert heat.

planting.note: Seed germinates best after a fall sowing outdoors or an equivalent cold-moist stratification, since it is native to montane sites with cold, snowy winters.

directions: Plant in lean, gravelly, fast-draining soil in full sun, replicating the dry montane slopes and pinyon-juniper woodlands of the Great Basin and California ranges where this species grows wild. Narrow, willowy stems carry slender scarlet-red flowers with a distinctive down-curved lower lip, a shape and color combination that makes it one of the most reliable hummingbird magnets among the western beardtongues. It tolerates poor, rocky soils that would starve most perennials and needs no supplemental water once established beyond an occasional deep soak in the driest years. Cut back spent flowering stems after bloom to keep the loosely branched habit tidy and to encourage a possible rebloom later in summer.

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall or provide 60-90 days of moist cold stratification before spring sowing; this high-elevation species needs winter chilling to germinate reliably.

directions: Grow in gritty, sharply draining soil in full sun, as in its native sagebrush flats and rocky slopes of Colorado, Utah, and Wyoming. This mat-forming, semi-woody beardtongue hugs the ground in a dense evergreen carpet studded with short spikes of violet-blue to lavender flowers in late spring, making it a durable choice for rock gardens, dry stone walls, and gravel paths where taller Penstemon species would flop. It is extremely drought tolerant once rooted in and shrugs off winter cold with ease, but resents wet feet, heavy clay, or summer humidity. Shear lightly after bloom only to remove spent flower stems; the foliage mat itself needs no regular maintenance.

common_name: Red Rocks Penstemon (Compact Rosy-Red Hybrid Beardtongue)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts or divisions in spring into gritty, well-drained soil; this Plant Select introduction is propagated vegetatively and does not come true from seed.

directions: Plant in lean to average, sharply draining soil in full sun; Red Rocks is a compact hybrid between Penstemon baccharifolius and P. triflorus selected in Colorado for exceptional heat and cold tolerance far beyond its Texas parentage. Dense spikes of deep rosy-red tubular flowers bloom continuously from early summer into fall, well past the single flush typical of most hardy beardtongues, and draw hummingbirds throughout the season. The tidy, low mounding habit and long bloom window make it a standout front-of-border xeriscape plant that needs no deadheading to keep flowering. Established plants tolerate both summer drought and winter wet better than most western Penstemon hybrids, but still perform best with a gravel mulch and minimal added fertility.
